```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Road segments, intersections or individuals observed repeatedly are not
independent, and the effect of a variable often differs from one unit to
another. flexCountReg handles both with random-parameter models
(`countreg.rp()`, also available as `countreg_rp()`) and random-effects
models (`renb()`, `poisLind.re()`, `repois()` and `negmultinom()`).

```{r setup}
library(flexCountReg)
```

## Why the panel structure matters: repeated seizure counts

`MASS::epil` records epileptic seizure counts for
`r length(unique(MASS::epil$subject))` patients in a clinical trial of
progabide (Thall and Vail, 1990). Each patient was observed in four
consecutive two-week periods, so there are four rows per patient. The
independent unit is the patient, not the row.

```{r epil}
epil <- MASS::epil
c(rows = nrow(epil), patients = length(unique(epil$subject)))
table(table(epil$subject))      # rows per patient
# treatment does not change within a patient
all(tapply(epil$trt, epil$subject, function(v) length(unique(v))) == 1)
```

The response `y` is the count in a two-week follow-up period. The count in
the eight-week *baseline* period before treatment (`base`) is a predictor,
not a response: MASS provides it as `lbase`, the centred logarithm of the
baseline count divided by 4 (a two-week equivalent), and the age as `lage`,
the centred log age. `V4` marks the fourth visit. (The data in MASS 7.3-65
and later include a documented correction to one count.)

A pooled model treats the 236 rows as independent; a random-effects model
(`renb()`, the negative binomial model of Hausman, Hall and Griliches,
1984) gives each patient a shared effect:

```{r epil-fits}
f_epil <- y ~ trt + lbase + lage + V4
pooled <- countreg(f_epil, data = epil, family = "NB2", method = "BFGS")
pooled_robust <- countreg(f_epil, data = epil, family = "NB2",
                          method = "BFGS", stderr = "robust")
panel <- renb(f_epil, group_var = "subject", data = epil, method = "BFGS")
se_trt <- function(m) sqrt(diag(vcov(m)))[["trtprogabide"]]
data.frame(
  model = c("pooled NB2", "pooled NB2, robust SE", "RENB (panel)"),
  treatment_effect = c(coef(pooled)[["trtprogabide"]],
                       coef(pooled_robust)[["trtprogabide"]],
                       coef(panel)[["trtprogabide"]]),
  std_error = c(se_trt(pooled), se_trt(pooled_robust), se_trt(panel)))
```

The pooled model's standard error for the treatment effect is
`r round(se_trt(pooled), 3)`, against `r round(se_trt(panel), 3)` in the
panel model. Rows from the same patient share that patient's seizure
tendency, so the pooled model counts four rows as four independent pieces of
evidence and overstates its precision. Robust standard errors computed row
by row (`r round(se_trt(pooled_robust), 3)`) do not fix this: they do not
group the rows by patient.

```{r epil-glance}
do.call(rbind, lapply(list(pooled = pooled, RENB = panel), function(m)
  glance(m)[, c("logLik", "AIC", "BIC", "nobs", "n_groups")]))
```

For panel models, `BIC()` uses the number of panels (`n_groups`,
`r glance(panel)$n_groups` patients) as the sample size, because the panels
are the independent units. The same unit applies to every form of
inference: the likelihood has one contribution per panel, robust standard
errors are clustered by panel, bootstrap standard errors resample whole
panels, and validation splits should keep each panel in one fold.

The rest of this vignette uses the `washington_roads` data:

```{r roads}
data("washington_roads")
length(unique(washington_roads$ID))   # road segments
nrow(washington_roads)                # segment-years
```

## Random-parameter models

In a random-parameter model, a coefficient varies across units:
$\beta_i = \mu + \sigma \upsilon_i$. With `group_var`, all observations
of a segment share one draw of the random parameter, which accounts for the
panel structure. The model is estimated by maximum simulated likelihood
with Halton draws; real analyses should use more draws (`ndraws`) than this
example, and check that the estimates are stable as the number grows.

```{r rp}
rp <- countreg_rp(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt, rpar_formula = ~ -1 + speed50,
                  data = washington_roads, family = "NB2",
                  rpardists = c(speed50 = "n"), offset = "lnlength",
                  group_var = "ID", ndraws = 100, method = "BFGS")
summary(rp)
```

`speed50:Mean` and `speed50:St.Dev` are the mean and standard deviation of
the speed-limit effect across segments. Distributions other than the normal
are available through `rpardists`. The two estimated parameters, labelled
`Mean` and `St.Dev`, do not always equal the actual mean and standard
deviation of the coefficient:

| `rpardists` | Coefficient | Actual mean | Actual SD |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"n"` normal | $\beta = \mu + \sigma z$ | $\mu$ | $\sigma$ |
| `"ln"` lognormal | $\beta = \exp(\mu + \sigma z)$ | $\exp(\mu + \sigma^2/2)$ | $\exp(\mu + \sigma^2/2)\sqrt{\exp(\sigma^2) - 1}$ |
| `"g"` gamma | gamma with mean $\mu$ and SD $\sigma$ | $\mu$ | $\sigma$ |
| `"t"` triangular | $\mu + \sigma T$, $T$ triangular on $[-1, 1]$ | $\mu$ | $\sigma/\sqrt{6}$ |
| `"u"` uniform | $\mu + \sigma U$, $U$ uniform on $[-1, 1]$ | $\mu$ | $\sigma/\sqrt{3}$ |

For the lognormal, $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are the mean and SD of $\log\beta$,
and the coefficient is positive; for a negative effect, enter the negative
of the variable. For the triangular and uniform, `St.Dev` is a half-width:
the coefficient lies in $[\mu - \sigma, \mu + \sigma]$.

### Heterogeneity in means

The mean of a random parameter can depend on covariates, following Wood and
Gayah (2025, Eq. 2): $\beta_i = \mu + z_i'\delta + \sigma\upsilon_i$.
Each random parameter gets its own coefficient for each heterogeneity
variable:

```{r het}
rp_het <- countreg_rp(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt, rpar_formula = ~ -1 + speed50,
                      het_mean_formula = ~ ShouldWidth04,
                      data = washington_roads, offset = "lnlength",
                      group_var = "ID", ndraws = 100, method = "BFGS")
tidy(rp_het)
```

### Predictions

There are three prediction methods for random-parameter models (Wood and
Gayah, 2025):

* `"Exact"` integrates over the random-parameter distributions analytically
  (with their moment generating functions), so it has no simulation error.
* `"Simulated"` averages over Halton draws.
* `"Individual"` (Empirical Bayes) uses each segment's observed crashes to
  estimate its own coefficients. It needs the outcome, so it is for data with
  observed outcomes.

```{r predict}
nd <- washington_roads[washington_roads$ID %in% unique(washington_roads$ID)[1:2], ]
cbind(observed = nd$Total_crashes,
      exact = predict(rp, newdata = nd, method = "Exact"),
      simulated = predict(rp, newdata = nd, method = "Simulated"),
      individual = predict(rp, newdata = nd, method = "Individual"))
```

The segment-specific coefficients from the Empirical Bayes method are
returned as an attribute:

```{r eb}
eb <- predict(rp, newdata = washington_roads, method = "Individual")
summary(attr(eb, "eb_coefficients")[, "speed50"])
```

A caution about the expected count: with a random parameter the expected
value of $\exp(x\beta)$ must exist. It is infinite when $\beta$ is
lognormal and $x > 0$, and when $\beta$ is gamma and
$x\sigma^2/\mu \ge 1$. In those cases `"Exact"` and `"Simulated"`
predictions return `Inf` with a warning (a simulated average would
otherwise depend on the number of draws without converging). This is a
property of the model, not a numerical failure: changing the distribution
only helps if the new distribution's expectation exists for the covariate
values used. Normal, triangular and uniform parameters always have a finite
expectation.

## Random-effects models

Random-effects models add a panel-level effect to every observation of a
unit. The negative binomial random-effects model of Hausman, Hall and
Griliches (`renb()`), the Poisson-Lindley random-effects model
(`poisLind.re()`) and the negative multinomial models (`negmultinom()`) are
available:

```{r re}
re_models <- list(
  RENB = renb(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + speed50, group_var = "ID",
              data = washington_roads, offset = "lnlength", method = "BFGS"),
  PoisLindRE = poisLind.re(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + speed50, group_var = "ID",
                           data = washington_roads, offset = "lnlength",
                           method = "BFGS"),
  NM2 = negmultinom(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + speed50, group_var = "ID",
                    data = washington_roads, offset = "lnlength")
)
do.call(rbind, lapply(names(re_models), function(nm) {
  cbind(model = nm,
        glance(re_models[[nm]])[, c("logLik", "AIC", "BIC", "nobs",
                                    "n_groups")])
}))
```

For panel models, `BIC()` uses the number of panels (`n_groups`) as the
sample size, because the panels are the independent units.

The warning above comes from the Poisson-Lindley random-effects model: its
random-effect parameter is driven toward the edge of its parameter space,
where the likelihood is flat, so its standard error is not identified and
is reported as `NA`:

```{r re-flat}
tidy(re_models$PoisLindRE)
```

Its fit statistics are close to those of the other two models, but with one
parameter not identified its reported uncertainty is incomplete. When models
fit about equally well, prefer one whose parameters are all identified, such
as RENB or the negative multinomial model here.

### Standard errors

The likelihood of a panel model has one contribution per panel, so robust
(sandwich) standard errors are clustered by panel. Bootstrap standard errors
resample whole panels:

```{r se}
re_robust <- poisLind.re(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + speed50, group_var = "ID",
                         data = washington_roads, offset = "lnlength",
                         method = "BFGS", stderr = "robust")
tidy(re_robust)
```

Cross-sectional models can also be fitted with `stderr = "robust"` or
`"boot"`; for repeated observations of the same units, prefer a panel model
or clustered resampling.

## Cross-validation

When tuning or comparing these models by cross-validation (for example with
the tidymodels `count_reg()` specification), resample whole panels, for
example with `rsample::group_vfold_cv(data, group = ID)`. Splitting the
observations of one segment between the training and test sets leaks
information and makes the models look better than they are.

Thall, P. F. and Vail, S. C. (1990). Some covariance models for longitudinal
count data with overdispersion. *Biometrics*, 46(3), 657-671.

Wood, J.S., & Gayah, V. (2025). Out-of-sample prediction and interpretation
for random parameter generalized linear models. *Accident Analysis and
Prevention*, 220, 108147.

Hausman, J. A., Hall, B. H., & Griliches, Z. (1984). Econometric models for
count data with an application to the patents-R&D relationship.
*Econometrica*, 52(4), 909-938.
